members.tone: Condemnation in an official voice - cruelty assessed rather than felt.
Condemns as a whole civilisation would: this is beneath what people owe each other.
Plain and physical, and the least ornamented of the strong words.
The central moral charge: the suffering was known about and inflicted anyway.
*One fell swoop* - on its own it reads as deliberate archaism.
*Ride roughshod over* - disregard rather than violence.
Brutality at full pitch - cruelty with restraint stripped away.
Adds enjoyment to the harm - a vicious act is one the doer wanted to do.
Puts the fault in the absence of ordinary human feeling, one step short of *bestial*.
Denies the person's humanity outright.
*Brute force* - unreasoning rather than wicked.
Coarse rather than violent: it says unrefined more than it says cruel.
The furthest word in the family - savagery named at its most extreme.
The absence of feeling, not its violence. A cold refusal need never raise its voice.
Premeditation is the whole charge - the harm was planned while calm.
Names what is missing rather than what was done; harsher than *inhumane*, which describes conditions.
The plain, unshowy word, and the one people most want said about them.
Literary and top-down - warmth extended by someone with the power not to bother.
Courtesy from a position of advantage; graciousness costs the giver nothing.
Mild kindness - gentler in force than 'benevolent', warmth without much heat.
Splits in two: charitable giving is warm, a *charitable interpretation* is faintly condescending.
Formal and settled - kindness as a disposition rather than a mood.
A gentler *kind* - the warmth is in the manner, not the deed.
Kindness aimed at someone in difficulty; it presumes there is trouble to meet.
Locates the kindness in the character, and forgives clumsiness in carrying it out.
Kindness without self-protection - the giver is not holding anything back.
Capacity, not just intent: there is room in this person for more than their own concerns.
Kindness expressed as restraint - the force that was available was not used.
Innate rather than practised; the kindness precedes the occasion for it.
The hyphenated spelling of the same word, equally warm.
Names one of the seven deadly sins; the excess is a moral failure, not an appetite.
Formal and disgusted, and about drink as much as food.
Describes the sick aftermath rather than the appetite - more pitiable than blamed.
Too bookish to wound - the oddity of the word softens the greed into comedy.
Literary and dry - hunger stated as if from a distance.
The hunger is predatory - devouring as though by seizure.
Predatory and archaic-sounding, as of a beast that has not eaten.
Hunger at full strength, and no fault in it.
Appetite at full stretch - the eating is hard to satisfy.
Adds hunger to the manner of eating; it watches the food the way a predator would.
The everyday charge for appetite: wanting more than one can use.
Compares the person to a pig outright, with none of the softening *piggy* has.
Greed and coarseness laid on with the farm animal - the comparison does the insulting.
Diminutive, and small enough to carry no real anger.
Formal and cold - the comparison to swine delivered clinically, which sharpens it.
Broader than eating: it condemns the whole manner of the person.
The plain word. Its mirror image is *thrifty*, which praises the identical behaviour.
Names the missing virtue rather than the present vice, which makes it the politer complaint.
Said of the sum, not the person - an amount so small it insults whoever receives it.
Of the amount, not the giver - a sum small enough to read as an insult.
Stinginess as a public embarrassment - the shame is the point.
Regional American and dismissive.
Stinginess with the embarrassment built in - the cheapness shows.
Formal and disdainful: economy pursued past the point of dignity.
Euphemistic. *Close with money* is what you say when you do not want to say stingy.
A euphemism - stinginess softened into mere 'closeness' with money.
Pictures the act, and the smallness of the coin does the condemning.
Stinginess as thinness - giving kept as lean as the frame.
The hand that will not open - refusal made physical.
Harder than 'closefisted' by a shade - the fist has closed tighter.
The most vivid of the fists - the hand is shut and stays shut.
The money was given - resentfully, which is what makes it worse than refusal for some.
The plain moral word - a direct accusation, nothing clinical in it.
It names a doctrine as much as a habit, which cools the accusation.
The same word with an extra syllable, and no extra force.
The clinical-sounding member of the family - reads as diagnosis more than accusation.
Softer than *selfish* - it describes where attention sits rather than what was taken.
The British spelling, identical in force.
Adds calculation: the generous-looking act had a private purpose.
The same charge, aimed at a career rather than a single act.
Vanity rather than greed - about talking of oneself, not taking for oneself.
Flat contempt for self-importance - the inflation is visible to everyone but its owner.
A clinical diagnosis used as an insult, which is what makes it land so hard.
The literal compound turned accusation - love pointed at the wrong object.
Inattentive rather than grasping; the harm is what gets overlooked.
The same forgivable fault, and the milder of the two phrasings.
Praise for modesty worn willingly - the opposite of arrogance, and credited for it.
Not modesty at all: something was done to this person and it worked.
The heaviest word in the family, and always about defeat rather than character.
Brought down and knowing it - the word reports the defeat and expects it to be admitted.
Requires an audience - the lowering had to be seen to count.
Status, not disposition - fallen in condition rather than in spirits.
Mildness that shades into submission - the virtue and the weakness share the word.
Gentleness of manner with no claim about the will behind it.
Approving of a retiring manner - mildness as virtue, though the gloss lets it border on submissiveness.
Formal and slightly distant - the complaint of someone invoking a standard.
The blunt word - it names the failure of manners without softening it.
The plain word for soiling - direct, and mildly reproachful.
Clinical and euphemistic - a softer word chosen to avoid 'dirty'.
Condemns the thing as unfit rather than merely dirty.
Pitiable rather than blamed - the rain did this, not the person.
A form of 'bedraggled', with the same sympathy for whatever got dragged through the mud.
Formal and disgusted, and it implies an agent: someone fouled this.
The plainer form of 'befouled' - the same dirtying stated without relish.
Heavy, literary dirt - ingrained past any quick washing.
Said of rooms and fabric, and the real complaint is that it is depressing.
Descriptive and physical; grime is a fact about a surface, not a fault.
Mild enough to be affectionate - dirt of the kind a child comes home in.
Informal and unimpressed - dirt that has been let settle in for good.
Dated - grime so thick it has worked into the thing itself.
Literal soot in this sense, and one of a great many senses this word carries.
Soot rather than filth - the dirt is superficial and comes off.
Disgust with a squirm in it - not merely dirty but inhabited.
The steady everyday word - a disposition rather than a burst of feeling.
The cheer has reached the face and is impossible to miss.
Quieter than 'happy' - cheer showing on the surface of things.
Storybook brightness - the smile is pure, quaint delight.
Describes the evidence rather than the mood, which is why it can be worn falsely.
Warm but faintly patronising - the warmth is being observed, not felt.
Sunny and unburdened - a lightness of spirit meant kindly.
The archaic-sounding form - it carries a deliberate literary flavour.
Free of weight rather than full of joy - the burden is what is missing.
Archaic in flavour - happiness carried as lightness.
The hyphenated spelling, identical in warmth.
Cheer that resists being pushed down; the metaphor is a thing that will not sink.
British and small-scale, and grating if the hearer is not cheerful too.
Brisk and a little relentless - it can condescend when said of an adult.
Outward-facing: a cheery greeting is aimed at somebody.
Brightness offered as cheer - the pleasure is in the surface, and is meant kindly.
The plain word and the strongest, because it needs no institution to make sense.
Formal - it names the duty rather than the feeling.
Devotion with the dignity taken out; praise and belittlement in the same word.
Intensity without direction - the loyalty is total, whatever it is to.
Loyalty at full strength - nothing held back and no way out.
Scottish and archaic - faithfulness with the ring of an old oath.
Feudal and historical: allegiance owed by rank, not chosen.
Loyalty proved and unswerving - steadfastness as identity.
